subQuestions.questionText:
Select the term in Column B that best matches the description in Column A. Write the letter of the term next to each description. Each letter may only be used once.

COLUMN A:
(a) Improved features in an organism as a result of cross breeding
(b) A characteristic that is influenced by genes on a gonosome
(c) A section of DNA that codes for a protein
(d) Having two different alleles for a particular gene
(e) An organism whose DNA has been altered using genetic engineering techniques
(f) Diagram to show the relatedness between individuals over generations
(g) The exchange of genes between homologous chromosomes
(h) A random change in the structure of a gene
(i) The physical site of a specific gene on a chromosome
(j) The condition in which a cell has more than two copies of each chromosome

COLUMN B:
A Sex-linked trait
B Heterozygous
C Mutation
D Locus
E Gene
F Polyploidy
G Diploid
H Hybrid vigour
I Family pedigree
J Genetically Modified Organism
K Crossing over
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) H — hybrid vigour
(b) A — sex-linked trait
(c) E — gene
(d) B — heterozygous
(e) J — genetically modified organism
(f) I — family pedigree
(g) K — crossing over
(h) C — mutation
(i) D — locus
(j) F — polyploidy
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
When a woman undergoes in vitro fertilisation (IVF) she is given a hormone to stimulate ovum development. What is this hormone?
A LH
B FSH
C Oestrogen
D Progesterone
subQuestions.memoText: B — FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) stimulates the development of the follicle and ovum.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.1 shows a foetus in the uterus, with four numbered areas (1–4). Which numbered area cushions and protects the foetus against physical injury?
A 1
B 2
C 3
D 4
(Refer to Figure 1.1 in the question paper — a developing foetus in the uterus.)
subQuestions.memoText: C — the amniotic fluid (amniotic cavity) cushions and protects the foetus against mechanical/physical injury.

subQuestions.questionText:
What is the main reason for the establishment of a seed bank?
A Educate societies on the importance of seeds as a food source.
B Sell seeds to agricultural companies for profit.
C Conduct hybridisation and genetic modification experiments.
D Store and preserve the genetic diversity of plant species.
subQuestions.memoText: D — a seed bank stores and preserves the genetic diversity of plant species (a safeguard against extinction and loss of biodiversity).

options.A: Educate societies on the importance of seeds as a food source.
options.B: Sell seeds to agricultural companies for profit.
options.C: Conduct hybridisation and genetic modification experiments.
options.D: Store and preserve the genetic diversity of plant species.

subQuestions.questionText:
Plant growth hormones promote growth and specialisation of cells. Why would farmers use these growth hormones?
A Limit the elongation and branching of stems.
B Reduce seed formation.
C Increase the number of flowers and fruit on plants.
D Delay the ripening of fruits in their fields.
subQuestions.memoText: C — farmers apply plant growth hormones (e.g. auxins/gibberellins) to increase the number of flowers and fruit and so raise crop yield.

options.A: Limit the elongation and branching of stems.
options.C: Increase the number of flowers and fruit on plants.
options.D: Delay the ripening of fruits in their fields.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which of the following is NOT a use of DNA profiling?
A Increasing the amount of DNA in samples.
B Paternity testing.
C Identifying the origins of illegally traded organisms.
D Analysing DNA samples from crime scenes.
subQuestions.memoText: A — increasing the amount of DNA in a sample is done by PCR (amplification), not by DNA profiling. B, C and D are all applications of DNA profiling.

options.A: Increasing the amount of DNA in samples.
options.C: Identifying the origins of illegally traded organisms.
options.D: Analysing DNA samples from crime scenes.

subQuestions.questionText:
Which technological process can be used to permanently change the genome?
A PCR
B Cloning
C SCNT
D CRISPR
subQuestions.memoText: D — CRISPR is a gene-editing tool that permanently alters the DNA sequence of the genome.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.2 shows the chromosomes in a cell at four stages of meiosis, labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4 (not in order). Which of the following is the correct sequence of events during meiosis?
A 1 2 3 4
B 3 4 1 2
C 3 1 4 2
D 4 1 2 3
(Refer to Figure 1.2 in the question paper — a cell shown at various phases of meiosis.)
subQuestions.memoText: B — 3 4 1 2 is the correct order of the meiotic phases shown.

subQuestions.questionText:
For each row, two items (1 and 2) are given with a term. Decide which item(s) relate to the term, using the codes:
A — only item 1 relates to the term
B — only item 2 relates to the term
C — both item 1 and item 2 relate to the term
D — neither item 1 nor item 2 relates to the term

(a) Term: Species. Item 1: Organisms that look similar. Item 2: Organisms able to breed with each other and produce fertile offspring.
(b) Term: Biogeography. Item 1: Distribution of similar species on different continents. Item 2: Sympatric speciation.
(c) Term: Darwin. Item 1: Inheritance of acquired characteristics. Item 2: Law of use and disuse of body structures.
(d) Term: Founder effect. Item 1: Limited gene flow. Item 2: Geographic isolation of a small group of individuals.
(e) Term: Divergent evolution. Item 1: Inbreeding. Item 2: Share a common ancestor.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) B or C — item 2 (interbreeding to produce fertile offspring) is the biological species definition; "look similar" alone is not sufficient.
(b) A — biogeography concerns the distribution of species across continents; sympatric speciation is not biogeography.
(c) D — inheritance of acquired characteristics and use and disuse are Lamarck's ideas, not Darwin's.
(d) C — both limited gene flow and geographic isolation of a small group describe the founder effect.
(e) B — divergent evolution is species sharing a common ancestor diverging; inbreeding is not divergent evolution.
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
A UN report showed that 65% of women relied on some form of contraception and 35% used none. Table 1 gives worldwide use and effectiveness of contraceptive methods:
Method | Worldwide use (%) | Effectiveness (%)
IUD | 15 | 99+
Oral Contraceptive Pill (OCP) | 20 | 99
Male condom | 15 | 93
Various other methods | 15 | 87
(remaining group) | 15 | 77

According to the table, which method is the most popular?
subQuestions.memoText: The oral contraceptive pill (OCP) — 20% worldwide use, the highest single value in the table.

subQuestions.questionText: Give TWO reasons why women may choose an IUD over the OCP as a means of birth control.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Does not require a daily reminder / very convenient
• Lasts a long time before replacement / long-term reliability
• More effective than the OCP (99% vs 93%)
• The OCP can have unpleasant side effects / has been linked to cancer
• Can lead to lighter, less painful periods
• Does not interfere with other medicines / antibiotics
• Woman takes full control of her own fertility

subQuestions.questionText: Male condom use in South Africa is about 60%. Suggest why this is much higher than the worldwide use.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• South Africa has a high HIV/AIDS and STI rate, so condoms are promoted to reduce transmission
• Condoms are cheap / distributed free from clinics
• Readily accessible / easily available
• Easy to use
• Condom use is heavily promoted through awareness campaigns

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE contraceptive method that would fall in the "various other methods" category listed in Table 1.
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE: rhythm method / spermicide / diaphragm / cervical cap / contraceptive injection / sterilisation (tubal ligation or vasectomy) / withdrawal / abstinence / female condom / hormonal IUD (Mirena).

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Table 1. Complete the pie chart provided to show the worldwide use for each contraceptive method.
subQuestions.memoText:
• Heading: e.g. "Pie chart showing worldwide use of contraceptive methods" (1)
• IUD segment ≈ 4 of the ~13 equal parts (largest at 20%) drawn correctly (OCP) — segment sizes proportional to the percentages (2)
• Any other method ≈ 3 parts each (15%) (1)
• At least two segments correctly labelled (1)

subQuestions.questionText: Huntington's Disease is caused by an autosomal dominant allele coding for an abnormal form of the huntingtin protein; the mutation involves the CAG DNA sequence being repeated. Explain what is meant by the term dominant allele.
subQuestions.memoText: A form / version / variant of a gene (1) that is expressed in the phenotype even in the heterozygous condition, masking the effect of the recessive allele (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Label the three parts of the nucleotide shown in the diagram (no heading required).
subQuestions.memoText:
• Phosphate (group)
• Deoxyribose / ribose / sugar
• Nitrogenous base (A / T / G / C / U)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Which nitrogenous base is only found in RNA?
subQuestions.memoText: Uracil (U).

subQuestions.questionText: Table 2 shows the amino acids coded for by mRNA codons. Using Table 2, determine how the amino acids would be different in the mutated section of mRNA compared with the normal section of mRNA.
subQuestions.memoText:
• In the mutated mRNA the codons code for Gln and Gln — glutamine is repeated (1).
• In the normal mRNA the codons code for Gln then Ala — glutamine is not repeated / is followed by a different amino acid (1).

subQuestions.questionText: How would the changed amino acid sequence affect the huntingtin protein?
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE: a longer polypeptide / an extra amino acid in the chain; the protein folds differently / takes on an abnormal shape; this changes (impairs) its function.

subQuestions.questionText: Construct a flow diagram to show how mRNA is formed from chromosomal DNA (transcription).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any 6 steps in a logical flow (6 marks):
• DNA unwinds and unzips / hydrogen bonds between the two strands break / strands separate
• RNA polymerase moves along / reads the DNA template strand
• Free RNA nucleotides align with the exposed DNA bases by complementary base pairing (A–U, G–C)
• A sugar-phosphate backbone links the nucleotides to form the new mRNA strand
• mRNA detaches from the DNA
• mRNA moves out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm; the DNA rewinds

subQuestions.questionText:
Three distantly related, geographically isolated leopard frog species (Rana spp.) with different ecological niches were studied; Figure 1.3 graphs the number of mating observations per month for each species. For each statement, decide whether it is:
A — supported by the information
B — contradicted by the information
C — neither supported nor contradicted by the information
(a) Rana berlandieri is observed to breed all year round.
(b) All three species of leopard frog live in the same ecological niche.
(c) Over 20 mating events were observed for Rana blairi.
(d) Rana sphenocephala only mates from January to March every year.
(Refer to Figure 1.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) A — supported
(b) B — contradicted (they have different ecological niches)
(c) A — supported
(d) B — contradicted
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Did the three species of leopard frog originate by allopatric or sympatric speciation? Give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Allopatric speciation (1) — the populations are geographically isolated from one another / occupy different (separate) ecological niches, preventing gene flow (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Researchers made plasticine models of white and brown mice and placed them in inland fields and on coastal sand dunes, recording the percentage of models attacked by predators (Figure 1.4).
(a) Identify the dependent variable in the investigation.
(b) What percentage of white mouse models were attacked in the sand dunes?
(c) Explain how the results support the researchers' hypothesis that predation drove the natural selection of mouse fur colour.
(Refer to Figure 1.4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) The percentage of (mouse models) attacked by predators (1).
(b) 28–32% (accept the value read from the graph) (1).
(c) Any 4 (4 marks): sand dunes are light-coloured while inland fields are darker; on the dunes brown fur is more visible to predators than white fur, while on inland fields white fur is more visible than brown; therefore more brown models were attacked on the dunes and more white models were attacked inland; e.g. ~70% of brown vs ~20% of white attacked on the coast — fur colour that matches the background is selected for.

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Darwin's theory of natural selection to explain how the population of mice on the coast evolved white fur.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any 5 (5 marks):
• There was variation in fur colour within the population
• Mice with lighter fur were better camouflaged against the white sand
• These mice had a greater chance of surviving and avoiding predation
• Surviving (white) mice reproduced more successfully
• The allele for light fur was passed on to more offspring
• Over many generations the proportion of light-furred individuals in the coastal population increased

subQuestions.questionText: Why is the change in fur colour NOT an example of macroevolution?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): only a small-scale change (fur colour only); occurred over a relatively short time; within a small population; no new species formed — it remains the same species (microevolution).

subQuestions.questionText:
Complete the table by choosing from the words in bold — Slow / Fast, Human / Environment, Decrease in variation / Increase in variation, Natural selection / Artificial selection — for each cell:
 | Natural selection column | Artificial selection column
1. Cause of change | ? | ?
2. Rate of change | ? | ?
3. Variation | ? | ?
subQuestions.memoText:
1. Cause of change: Environment (natural selection) | Human (artificial selection)
2. Rate of change: Slow (natural selection) | Fast (artificial selection)
3. Variation: Increase in variation (natural selection) | Decrease in variation (artificial selection)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.5 shows the female reproductive system with numbered parts (1–6). Choose the number that corresponds with each statement:
(a) Non-permanent layer richly supplied with blood vessels.
(b) Muscle action and cilia move the developing zygote to the uterus.
(c) Place where sperm is deposited during sexual intercourse.
(d) Cavity where the foetus grows and develops during gestation.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) 6 — endometrium
(b) 4 — Fallopian tube / oviduct
(c) 1 — vagina
(d) 5 — uterus
(1 mark each; numbers as per the memo key)

subQuestions.questionText:
On the diagram of the female reproductive system, indicate ONE place where each of the following occurs:
(a) Place an "X" where ovulation takes place.
(b) Place an "M" where implantation would occur in a healthy pregnancy.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) "X" placed on an ovary (1).
(b) "M" placed anywhere on the endometrium / lining of the uterus (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Turner syndrome is a disorder caused by a chromosomal mutation affecting females; symptoms are caused by the loss of genetic information during meiosis when chromosomes fail to separate properly. It is not hereditary and occurs by chance. A karyotype can be made from foetal cells (Figure 2.1). Where in the cell would chromosomes be located?
subQuestions.memoText: In the nucleus / nucleoplasm.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the term used to describe chromosomes numbered 1 to 22.
subQuestions.memoText: Autosomes.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the chromosomal abnormality seen in the Turner syndrome karyotype in Figure 2.1.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): one sex chromosome (gonosome) instead of two / the second X is missing; only 45 chromosomes are present instead of 46; the gonosomes are not a homologous pair; aneuploidy of the sex chromosomes (monosomy X, 45,X).

subQuestions.questionText: Were these chromosomes taken from a somatic cell or a gamete? Give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: Somatic cell (1). Reason (1): homologous chromosomes are present / the cell is (near-)diploid with two of each homologue; a gamete would contain only 23 single (unpaired) chromosomes.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain clearly why Turner syndrome is not an inherited condition.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): it does not run in families / is not passed from parent to offspring; it arises by chance from non-disjunction of the gonosomes during meiosis (a random event in gamete formation); affected individuals are usually sterile and so cannot pass it on.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why a karyotype analysis for genetic disorders is not routinely offered to all pregnant women.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): obtaining foetal cells is an invasive procedure that can cause miscarriage; it is expensive; it requires expertise/facilities that are not widely available; such mutations are rare, so it is not needed where there is no family history; risk is low in young mothers.

subQuestions.questionText:
From the source on Turner syndrome, name:
(a) the gland that secretes growth hormone.
(b) two ovarian hormones that would require hormone replacement therapy.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) The pituitary gland / hypophysis (1).
(b) Oestrogen and progesterone (1 mark each).

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest any TWO areas of training that are important for a genetic counsellor to become a skilled professional.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): genetics / inheritance; medical training; psychology / counselling; social work.

subQuestions.questionText:
Growth hormone can be produced for people who under-secrete it, using recombinant DNA technology (Figure 2.2, steps 1–5).
(a) Name the enzyme that 'cuts' the DNA in steps 2 and 4.
(b) Name the enzyme used in step 5 and explain its role in recombinant DNA technology.
(c) Why are bacteria useful organisms for recombinant DNA technology?
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Restriction enzyme / restriction endonuclease (1).
(b) (DNA) ligase (1); it joins / seals the gene (piece of DNA) into the plasmid (bacterial DNA) (1).
(c) Any 2 (2 marks): bacteria reproduce rapidly so many copies of the gene/protein are made quickly; they reproduce asexually so all offspring are genetically identical and contain the recombinant gene; they are cheap and readily available; large quantities of the human protein can be produced; bacteria naturally have plasmids that make gene transfer easy.

subQuestions.questionText: The thyroid gland is made of thyroid sacs lined by cuboidal cells that secrete thyroxin. Micrographs of thyroid tissue from a sick cat and a healthy cat are provided. State ONE function of the hormone thyroxin.
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE: increases / controls the metabolic rate; controls the rate of cellular respiration; promotes normal heart function; promotes normal nervous system function.

subQuestions.questionText: List ONE symptom of an under-secretion of thyroxin.
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE: physical/mental tiredness (lethargy); low blood pressure; low body temperature; low heart rate; low respiratory rate; weight gain.

subQuestions.questionText: Tabulate TWO differences seen in the thyroid tissue of the sick cat compared with the healthy cat.
subQuestions.memoText:
Table with a heading and comparable pairs (5 marks: 1 for table format/heading + 2 comparable differences × 2). Examples:
Sick cat thyroid tissue | Healthy cat thyroid tissue
Fewer, larger blood capillaries | Many, smaller blood capillaries
Fewer, larger thyroid sacs | Many, smaller thyroid sacs
Fewer / larger cuboidal (thyroxin-secreting) cells | Many / smaller cuboidal cells

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the actual length of the lumen of the thyroid sac from X to Y in the sick cat micrograph. Show all working. (The scale bar represents 50 µm.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Working (4 marks):
• Measure line X–Y ≈ 51–53 mm (accept range)
• Measure the scale bar ≈ 21–23 mm
• Actual length = (X–Y measurement ÷ scale-bar measurement) × 50 µm
• ≈ 110–126 µm (≈ 0,11–0,12 mm). Answer must include a unit; accept the range and answers in mm.

subQuestions.questionText: Why are many blood capillaries found in the thyroid tissue?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): thyroxin is a hormone that is transported in the blood — the thyroid is an endocrine (ductless) gland that secretes directly into the blood; capillaries also deliver nutrients and oxygen to the active secretory cells and remove waste.

subQuestions.questionText:
The vet hypothesised that the sick cat has a non-functioning thyroid gland. Iodine is absorbed from the blood by the thyroid and used to make thyroxin. Both cats were given radioactive iodine and the percentage remaining in the blood was measured over 80 hours. In the graph, the sick cat's line stays above 80% while the healthy cat's line falls below 20%.
(a) Provide a suitable title for the graph.
(b) Do the results indicate that the sick cat has a non-functioning thyroid gland? Provide reasons from the graph.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Title (3 marks — must name both variables and both cats): e.g. "Graph showing the percentage of radioactive iodine remaining in the blood of a sick cat and a healthy cat over time (hours) after injection."
(b) Yes (4 marks — any 4): the percentage of radioactive iodine in the sick cat's blood stayed high (above 80%), showing the iodine was not taken up by its thyroid gland; so little or no thyroxin is produced / metabolism impaired; in the healthy cat the percentage in the blood dropped (below 20%) after ~30 hours, showing iodine was absorbed by its thyroid and used to make thyroxin.

subQuestions.questionText: The tuatara is a New Zealand land vertebrate, the only living member of the order Rhynchocephalia, and an important link to the extinct reptiles from which dinosaurs, modern reptiles, birds and mammals evolved. Scientists sequenced its genome in partnership with indigenous Māori tribe members. Give the meaning of the term genome.
subQuestions.memoText: The complete set of genes / genetic material (DNA) in a cell / organism / species (2 marks).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain your understanding of what is meant by "scientists sequenced the genome of the tuatara".
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): they determined the order of all the bases (nucleotides) in the DNA; identified all the genes and their positions (loci) on the chromosomes; and/or worked out the functions of the genes / the proteins they code for.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the phylogenetic tree in Figure 3.2:
(a) How long ago did the tuatara and the python share a common ancestor?
(b) Explain why the evolution of Dasypus and Loxodonta can be described as an example of punctuated equilibrium and not gradualism.
(c) Why is the tuatara more closely related to the serpent (Serpentes) lineage than the crocodile (Crocodilia) lineage?
(Refer to Figure 3.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) About 250 million years ago (2).
(b) Any 2 (2 marks): Dasypus and Loxodonta diverged from a common ancestor over a short period of time (rapid change, ~90 mya) and their lineages then remained largely unchanged for long periods — gradualism would require small continuous changes over a much longer time.
(c) They share a more recent common ancestor (with the Serpentes lineage) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the amniotic egg is viewed as a "major evolutionary step" by scientists.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (4 marks): organisms are no longer dependent on water bodies for reproduction, so they can breed and live fully on land; the embryo has its own food supply within the egg; the shell (or uterus) protects the embryo and prevents it from drying out (desiccation); reduces competition for and predation in water pools where larvae would develop; the embryo can develop further before hatching.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why it was important that the scientists in the study partnered with the local indigenous people, the Māori.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): to share information and gain valuable indigenous knowledge about the tuatara (e.g. locations); to build trust and collaboration with the community; it is ethical to include the guardians of the species; it promotes conservation and protection of biodiversity; it avoids conflict.

subQuestions.questionText: "Little Foot" is a nearly complete Australopithecus fossil skeleton found in 1994–1998 in the Sterkfontein caves, South Africa; from the four ankle bones it was determined that Little Foot could walk upright. Give the term used to describe the ability to walk upright.
subQuestions.memoText: Bipedalism (bipedal).

subQuestions.questionText: List three features of the skeleton that would suggest to scientists that Little Foot walked upright.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (1 mark each): forward (central) position of the foramen magnum; short, broad, bowl-shaped pelvis; S-shaped (curved) spine; legs longer than arms; large heel bone; big toe aligned with the other toes (non-opposable); arched foot; femur angled inwards towards the knee.

subQuestions.questionText: Describe TWO advantages of being able to walk upright for early hominids.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): frees the arms/hands to carry food, offspring, tools or weapons; allows the animal to see further (over grass) to spot predators or prey; reduces the body surface area exposed to the sun (less overheating); bipedal walking is more energy-efficient over long distances.

subQuestions.questionText: Why do caves like the Sterkfontein system provide ideal locations for finding fossils?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): hominids used caves as shelter, or fell into them and died there; the high mineral (e.g. calcium/lime) content and presence of water promote fossilisation; remains are protected from scavengers and weathering; the low-oxygen environment slows decay.

subQuestions.questionText:
Little Foot was unveiled in 2017 by Prof. Ron Clarke after 20 years of excavation; first dated to ~2,2 mya (suggesting Australopithecus africanus) but now dated to 3,67 mya, and reclassified as Australopithecus prometheus. State how THREE labelled structures of the Little Foot skull differ in a human skull.
(Refer to Figure 3.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (1 mark each): brow ridge smaller/less pronounced in humans (more pronounced in Little Foot); mandible (jaw) smaller in humans (larger in Little Foot); cranium larger in humans (smaller in Little Foot); face more vertical in humans (sloping/prognathous in Little Foot).

subQuestions.questionText: How have African fossils like Little Foot contributed to our understanding of hominid evolution?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): support the "Out of Africa" hypothesis (Africa as the cradle of humankind); help establish the relatedness and a timeline of extinct hominids; fill gaps in the fossil record; give insight into how and where early hominids lived and into environmental changes linked to physical changes; help identify the oldest extant populations.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why it took over 20 years for the scientists to reveal the complete Little Foot skeleton to the public.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): the excavation was extremely difficult and slow (bones embedded in hard rock/breccia); cleaning, preparing and cataloguing the fossils is painstaking and time-consuming; dating, verification and collaboration with other scientists, and peer review before publication, all take time; dating technology improved over the period.

subQuestions.questionText: Why did Ron Clarke reclassify Little Foot as Australopithecus prometheus?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): the skull bones and teeth are so unusual / different from Australopithecus africanus that they suggest a distinct species; Little Foot is dated older (3,67 mya) than A. africanus.

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE other fossil example of Australopithecus africanus.
subQuestions.memoText: Mrs Ples (or the Taung Child).

subQuestions.questionText: Study Figure 3.4 (changes in biological and cultural evolution over millions of years). Explain the relationship between hominid evolution and practices such as tool making.
subQuestions.memoText: As biological (hominid) evolution increased — e.g. increasing brain size — the rate of cultural evolution such as tool making also increased: a positive relationship between the two variables (2 marks — name both variables and the relationship).

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO ways in which an increase in brain size in hominids impacted cultural practices.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 ideas, each developed (2 marks each): development of weapons/better tools improved hunting and access to protein/fat-rich food, butchering, carrying food, building shelters and making clothes; control of fire allowed cooking (better nutrition) and social/ceremonial gatherings; language development enabled oral tradition, storytelling and communication; use of pigments and objects led to art, jewellery, bead-making and rock painting / recording information — greater creativity.

subQuestions.questionText: Sea urchins have separate sexes; males release millions of sperm and females release thousands of eggs directly into the water, where currents transport the gametes, and only a small percentage of eggs are fertilised (Figure 4.1). Does the sea urchin have internal or external fertilisation? Give a well-explained reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: External fertilisation (1). Reason (2): the sperm and eggs are released into the water and the sperm fuses with the egg outside the female's body.

subQuestions.questionText: Why are sea urchins suitable animals to use in fertility studies?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): easy to keep in aquaria; release sperm readily; gametes are easy to collect; external fertilisation is easy to observe and monitor; their gametes are similar to human gametes.

subQuestions.questionText:
Sea urchin sperm is similar in structure to human sperm.
(a) Name the organ where sperm cells are produced in humans.
(b) Draw a diagram of a human sperm cell. Provide THREE suitable labels.
(c) Do you think studying reproduction in sea urchins would be valuable to understanding more about human reproduction? Explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) The testes (1).
(b) Diagram (5 marks): correct overall shape with head and a much longer tail (proportion) (1); acrosome shown at the tip of the head (1); 3 correct labels e.g. acrosome, nucleus (head), mitochondria (mid-piece), tail/flagellum (3).
(c) A reasoned answer (2 marks). Yes: sea urchin gametes and early embryo development are similar to and easy to observe, with fewer ethical concerns and no humans harmed. OR No: sea urchins are very different (not mammals), with external fertilisation and ovipary, so development differs from internal fertilisation and vivipary in humans.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why human sperm cells contain many more mitochondria than sea urchin sperm cells.
subQuestions.memoText: Human sperm need more energy (ATP) (must have) (1); any one further point (1): they must swim a much greater distance through the female reproductive tract; they cannot rely on water currents; the mucus/fluid they move through is denser than water, so more energy is needed for propulsion.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 4.2 shows three survivorship curves (A, B and C). Suggest which line would represent sea urchins and provide reasons about sea urchin reproduction to support your answer.
(Refer to Figure 4.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Line C (1) plus any 3 reasons (3): sea urchins produce very large numbers of offspring; most offspring die young / are eaten by predators; very few survive to reach maximum lifespan; there is no parental care, so mortality is highest early in life.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mendel used ~30 000 garden pea plants, which naturally self-fertilise to give true-breeding (homozygous) plants, and performed hybridisations between homozygous plants with contrasting traits. Figure 4.3 shows a longitudinal section of a pea flower with parts A–D. Provide labels for parts A to D.
(Refer to Figure 4.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
A: ovule
B: ovary
C: filament
D: stigma
(1 mark each; labels as per the memo key.)

subQuestions.questionText: What is the function of the part labelled D (stigma)?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): produces a sticky secretion that receives/traps pollen grains (the site of pollination); the site where pollen germinates.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the type of section represented by the flower in Figure 4.3.
subQuestions.memoText: Longitudinal section.

subQuestions.questionText: State the letter from Figure 4.3 that contains the female gametes.
subQuestions.memoText: A (the ovule).

subQuestions.questionText:
Mendel crossed plants homozygous dominant for purple flowers (A) with plants recessive for white flowers (a); the F1 and F2 ratios are shown.
(a) State the genotype of the plant with white flowers in the parental generation.
(b) Draw a Punnett diagram to illustrate the F1 × F1 cross. Give the genotypic results of the F2 generation.
(c) How did Mendel ensure that he controlled cross-pollination in his breeding experiments?
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) aa / homozygous recessive (1).
(b) F1 is Aa; cross Aa × Aa. Punnett square gametes A, a on each axis giving AA, Aa, Aa, aa (Punnett square correct — 1 per correct row, up to the allocated marks); genotypic ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (25% : 50% : 25%) (6 total).
(c) Any 2 (2 marks): removed/cut the anthers (emasculated) from the flowers to prevent self-pollination; then hand-pollinated using pollen from the chosen parent plant.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss how the results of Mendel's experiments advanced our knowledge of modern genetics.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (4 marks): showed that traits are controlled by two discrete factors (alleles) that do not blend; one factor can be expressed (dominant) while the other is masked (recessive); the pairs of factors separate (segregate) randomly during gamete formation (Law of Segregation); his experiments were carefully designed with large numbers, are repeatable, and the results are still trusted and applied today.
